paragraphs.text:
OF JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, ARCHBISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, ON VIRGINITY.

1. The Jews turn away from the beauty of virginity. That is no wonder, since they dishonoured even Christ himself, who was born of a Virgin. The Greeks admire it and are amazed by it, but only the Church of God strives for it. I would never call the virgins of the heretics virgins. First, they are not chaste, because they have not been betrothed to one husband, as Christ's blessed bridal escort wishes when he says, "I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." Even if this was said of the whole fullness of the Church, the saying still includes those women too. So how could women be chaste who do not cherish the one husband, but bring in beside him another god who does not exist? That is the first reason why they would not be virgins. The second is that they came to abstain from marriage only after dishonouring it. By laying down as law that the thing is evil, they forestalled themselves and robbed themselves of the prizes of virginity. For people who abstain from bad things, it would be just only that they not be punished, not that they be crowned. One can see this arranged in the same way not only in our laws but also in the laws of outsiders. "Let the murderer be put to death," it says, but it does not add, "Let the one who does not murder be honoured." "Let the thief be punished," but they did not also order that the one who does not damage other people's property receive a gift. And while they put the adulterer to death, they did not think the one who does not break into other people's marriages worthy of any honour. And very reasonably so. For praise and admiration belong to those who accomplish good things, not to those who [?]

[?] and it is [?] to love one's enemies. Since we have agreement on this point from every side, let the heretics stop wearing themselves out for nothing. They will receive no reward. This is not because the Lord is unjust, perish the thought, but because they themselves are senseless and wicked. How so? It has been shown that no gift is laid up for merely avoiding bad things. But they fled marriage because they thought it bad. How then can they demand a reward for withdrawing from bad things? We will not claim to be crowned for not committing adultery, and neither will they for not marrying. For on that day the one who judges us will say to them: "I have not appointed honours only for those who abstained from wicked things (in my sight that part is a small thing). It is those who pursued every virtue whom I bring into the ageless inheritance of heaven. How then can you, who thought marriage an unclean and accursed thing, demand for your release from accursed things the prizes laid up for those who work at what is good?" This is why he sets the lambs on his right, blesses them and brings them into the kingdom. It is not because they did not seize what belonged to others, but because they shared what was their own with others. And he welcomes the one who was entrusted with five talents. It is not because he did not reduce what was given, but because he increased it and returned the deposit doubled. How long, then, will you keep running in vain, toiling to no purpose, boxing aimlessly and beating the air? If only it were merely in vain! Yet even that is no small punishment: to have toiled hard, to have expected prizes greater than the toil, and then, when the time of honour comes, to be ranked among the dishonoured.

2. But that is not the only terrible thing now, and their loss does not stop at gaining nothing. Other things far harsher than these await them: the unquenchable fire, the undying worm, the outer darkness, affliction and distress. So we would need ten thousand mouths and the power of angels to give God fitting thanks for his care for us. Or rather, even that would not be enough. How could it be? The toil for virginity is the same for us and for the heretics, and perhaps even much greater for them. But the fruit of the toil is not the same. For them there are chains and tears and wailing and endless punishment. For us there are the portions of the angels, the bright lamps, and, the crown of all good things, life with the Bridegroom. Why, then, do the same labours bring opposite rewards? Because they chose virginity in order to make laws against God, while we practise it in order to fulfil his will. That God wishes all people to abstain from marriage, our witness is the one who had Christ speaking in him: "For I wish," he says, "that all people were as I myself am," that is, in continence. But our Saviour spared us. He knew that the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak, so he did not shut the matter up within the compulsion of a commandment, but left the choice of it to our souls. For if it were a command and a law, those who achieved it would not have enjoyed honour, but would have heard, "What you were obliged [to do...]" [?] [Apparatus, garbled: "...the sheep on the right. Below, after 'talents' [?] in Reg. [?] ...prizes, when the time has come. The heretics are punished for having practised virginity. [?] For the toil... clearly 'in continence'. Spar[ing]..."]

[?] For the chastity of the heretics is worse than any licentiousness. Licentiousness limits its wrongdoing to human beings, but their chastity fights against God and insults his infinite wisdom. Such are the snares the devil sets for those who serve him. That the virginity of the heretics is precisely an invention of his wickedness is not my claim, but that of the one who was not ignorant of the devil's designs. What does he say? "The Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith. They will pay attention to deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose own consciences are seared. These forbid marriage and order abstinence from foods which God created to be received." How then is she a virgin who has departed from the faith, who pays attention to deceivers, obeys demons and honours falsehood? How is she a virgin whose conscience is seared? A virgin must be pure not only in body but also in soul, if she is to receive the holy Bridegroom. How could this woman be pure, branded as she is so many times? Even worldly cares must be driven out of this bridal chamber, since one cannot remain seemly with them. How then can the beauty of virginity be kept safe when an ungodly mind is turning things over within?

6. Even if her body remains intact, the better part is still corrupted, namely the thoughts of the soul. What use is it for the enclosure walls to stand when the temple has been destroyed? Or what is gained if the place of the throne is clean when the throne itself is defiled? Or rather, even so the place is not free of defilement. For blasphemy and wicked words are born within, but they do not stay within the soul. Uttered through the mouth, they defile the tongue, and they defile the ear that receives them. Like poisons falling into the soul itself, they eat through the root more cruelly than any moth, and with it they destroy the whole rest of the body. If, then, the definition of virginity is to be holy in both body and spirit, and this woman is profane and accursed in both, how could she be a virgin? "But she shows me a pale face, wasted limbs, a cheap robe and a gentle look." What use is that, when the inner eye is brazen? What could be more brazen than the gaze that persuades even the outward eyes to look on God's creatures as evil? "All the glory of the king's daughter is within." But she has turned the saying upside down: she wears the glory on the outside and keeps all the dishonour within. This is the terrible thing: toward people she shows great modesty, but toward God who created her she acts with great madness. She cannot bear even to look a man in the face (if indeed there are any such among them), yet she looks at the Master of humankind with shameless eyes and speaks unrighteousness against the One on high. Their faces are the colour of boxwood and like a corpse's. That is why they deserve tears and much lament: they have taken on so great a hardship not only in vain, but to their ruin and on their own heads.

7. Her robe is cheap. But virginity is not in clothes or colours; it is in body and soul. Would it not be absurd if we tested a philosopher not by his hair, nor by his staff, nor by his cloak, but by his ways [?] [Apparatus, garbled: "[?] alone: 'she who pays attention to deceit.' The same alone shortly after: 'demons' [?]."]

[?] you say is [?], the achievement no longer comes from your free choice but from the compulsion of the law. That is why we admire Persians who do not marry their mothers, but not Romans. Here everyone without exception thinks the thing loathsome, but there the impunity of those who dare it has made those who abstain from such unions praiseworthy. By the same reasoning we must examine the case of marriage too. Among us the thing is permitted to everyone, so we rightly admire those who do not marry. But you have thrust it among the worse things, so you can no longer lay claim to the praise that comes from refraining. Abstaining from what is forbidden is not yet the mark of a noble and vigorous soul. Perfect virtue does not lie in not doing things that would make everyone think us wicked if we did them. It lies in excelling in things that do not let those who did not choose them be reproached for it, while those who chose and achieved them are not only freed from a bad reputation but enrolled among the good. No one would praise eunuchs for virginity just because they do not marry, and no one would praise you either. What the necessity of nature is for them, the prejudice of a wicked conscience has become for you. The maiming of their bodies has shut eunuchs out from the honour of the deed. In the same way the devil, though your nature remains intact, has cut away your right reasoning and so put you under the necessity of not marrying. He stretches you on the rack of labours, but does not let you be honoured. You forbid marriage? Then no reward will be laid up for you for not marrying, but rather retribution and punishment.

9. "But you," he says, "do you not forbid it?" Perish the thought! May I never be as mad as you! "How then," he says, "can you urge people not to marry?" Because I am convinced that virginity is far more honourable than marriage. Yet that is no reason for me to count marriage among evil things. On the contrary, I praise it highly. For those who wish to use it well, it is a harbour of chastity that does not let nature run wild. It sets lawful intercourse before us like a breakwater, takes the waves of desire upon it, and so settles us and keeps us in great calm. But there are some who do not need this safeguard. Instead, they tame the madness of nature with fasts, vigils, sleeping on the ground and the rest of a harsh discipline. These I advise not to marry, without forbidding them to marry. There is a great difference between the two, as great as the difference between compulsion and free choice. The one who advises leaves the hearer free to choose in the matters on which he gives advice. The one who forbids takes away that very freedom. Besides, when I give advice, I do not denounce the thing, and I do not accuse the one who is not persuaded. But you slander it, call it bad, and seize the role of a lawgiver rather than an adviser, so naturally you hate those who are not persuaded. I do not. I admire those who have entered this contest, but I do not accuse those who stay outside the games. Accusation is just when someone leans toward an evil that everyone acknowledges. But one who has the lesser good and does not reach the greater is deprived of sharing in the other's praise and admiration; it would not be just to accuse him. How then do I forbid marriage, when I do not accuse those who marry? I forbid fornication and adul[tery]... [Apparatus: "Reg.: 'which does not let even those who did not choose...' Reg.: 'takes this freedom from him.'"]

[?] But the virgins of the Church will be met by the many great good things that pass beyond the human eye and ear and mind. So let us leave those people aside (enough has been said to them) and speak with the children of the Church.

12. Where, then, is it good to begin our discourse? With the very words of the Lord, which he speaks through blessed Paul, for we must believe that Paul's exhortation is the Lord's exhortation. When he says, "To the married I give this command, not I but the Lord," and again, "To the rest I say, not the Lord," he does not mean that his own words are one thing and the Lord's another. He had Christ speaking in him. He was eager not even to live himself, so that Christ might live in him. He placed the kingdom and life and angels and powers and any other created thing, simply everything, second to love for Christ. How could such a man have brought himself to say, or even to think, anything that did not please Christ, and that while laying down law? What, then, does he mean by "I" and "not I"? Of the laws and doctrines, Christ gave us some through himself and some through the apostles. To see that he did not lay them all down himself, hear what he says: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now." He himself had already made the law that a wife should not separate from her husband, while he was on earth in the flesh. That is why Paul says, "To the married I give this command, not I but the Lord." But about unbelievers Christ said nothing to us in his own person. Instead he moved Paul's soul to it and made the law that way. That is why Paul said, "Not the Lord, but I." He did not wish to show that what was said was human (how could it be?), but that Christ had not given this commandment when he was present with the disciples, but was giving it now through Paul. "The Lord, not I" is not the speech of someone opposing Christ's command. In the same way, "I, not the Lord" is not the speech of someone saying something of his own against what pleased God; it only shows that the commandment is now being given through him. For when he discusses the widow, he says, "She is happier if she remains as she is, in my judgment." Then, so that hearing "my judgment" you would not think the reasoning human, he cut off the suspicion with an addition: "And I think that I too have the Spirit of God." He speaks the things of the Spirit and calls it his own judgment, yet we will not say for that reason that the ruling is human. So too now, when he says, "I say, not the Lord," do not think for that reason that the word is Paul's. He had Christ speaking in him, and he would not have dared to lay down so great a doctrine as a binding ruling unless he was bringing the law to us from there. For someone might have said to him: "I cannot bear it, as a believer, to live with an unbelieving wife, the pure with the accursed. You yourself said beforehand that this is you speaking, not the Lord. Where, then, is my security and certainty?" But Paul would have answered him: "Do not fear. This is why I said that Christ [?]..." [Apparatus, garbled: "...made the law, saying, 'If anyone has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not divorce her.' That is why Paul too said ... 'And a woman who has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not divorce him.' That is why, then, he said [?] ... Regius [?]; in the margin: 'discussing the widow' ... 'do not fear' [?] ... Plautius [?] and 'he explained' [?]."]

"I would not have dared to lead you up to this lofty summit, because the thing is so hard to achieve. But since you wrote to me first, I give my advice with confidence." Why else, when they had written to him about many things, did he add this nowhere else? For no other reason than the one I have just given. So that no one would resent the exhortation, he reminds them of the letter they had sent. Even so, he does not press the exhortation forcefully, though he had been given such an opening, but gives it very gently. In this too he imitates Christ, for the Saviour also, after finishing his discourse on virginity, added, "Let the one who can accept it accept it." What, then, does Paul say? "Now concerning the things you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman."

14. But perhaps someone will say: "If it is good not to touch a woman, why did marriage come into life? What use will we have for a woman from now on, if she serves us neither for marriage nor for having children? What will stop the whole human race from being wiped out? Death eats it away and cuts it down every day, and this teaching does not let others rise up in place of those who fall. If we all strive for this good and do not touch women, everything will be gone: cities, houses, fields, crafts, animals, plants. When the general falls, the good order of the army must break apart. In the same way, once man, who rules over everything on earth, has been wiped out through not marrying, none of the rest will stay in the same security and good order, and this fine precept will fill the world with countless evils." Now if these words came only from enemies and unbelievers, I would take little account of them. But many who seem to belong to the Church say these things too. Through weakness of will they have fallen short of the sweat that virginity demands. By disparaging the thing and declaring it superfluous, they want to cover up their own laziness, so that they will seem to have fallen behind in these contests not through negligence but through sound judgment. So come, let us leave the enemies aside ("for the unspiritual man does not receive the things of the Spirit, since they are foolishness to him"). Let us teach those who pretend to be on our side two things. First, the thing is not superfluous but in fact very useful and necessary. Second, such an accusation does not leave them unharmed, but will bring them as much danger as it brings reward and praise to those who achieve it. When this whole world had been completed, and everything for our rest and use had been made ready, God formed man, for whose sake he had also made the world. Once formed, man stayed in paradise, and there was no mention of marriage. He needed a helper too, and she came into being. Even then marriage did not seem necessary. Indeed, it had not yet even appeared. They remained without it, living in paradise as if in heaven and delighting in converse with God. Desire for intercourse, conception, birth pangs, childbirth and every form of corruption were banished from their souls. Like a clear stream flowing from a pure spring, so were they in that place by [?]... [Apparatus, garbled: "[?] 'dared'. Below [?] 'advice' [?] 'to touch. For why' ... 'of the commands, as ... which they sent.' ...'birth pangs'? Because these things were then superfluous, but later... Reg.: 'beauty'."]

…have become necessary because of our weakness: these things, and all the others too — cities, crafts, the wearing of clothes and the rest of the crowd of needs. For death dragged all these in with it when it entered. So do not prefer what was permitted because of your weakness to virginity, or rather, do not even put the two on an equal footing. If you follow this reasoning, you will also say that having two wives is better than being content with one, since this too was permitted in the law of Moses. In the same way you will prefer wealth to voluntary poverty, luxury to a temperate diet, and retaliation to bearing nobly with the one who wrongs you.

16. “But you disparage these things,” someone says. Not at all. God permitted them, and they were useful in their time. But I say that they are small things, the achievements of children rather than of men. And for this reason Christ, wishing to make us perfect, commanded us to put those things aside like children's clothes, which cannot clothe the perfect man or adorn the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. Instead he commanded us to put on things more becoming and more perfect than those. In this he was not legislating against himself; on the contrary, he was entirely consistent. For even if these commands are greater than those, the lawgiver's purpose is the same. What is that purpose? To prune away the wickedness of our soul and lead it to perfect virtue. If, then, he had been intent not on enjoining things greater than before but on leaving us forever in the same state, and never freeing us from that meanness, he would have been flatly contradicting himself. Suppose that at the beginning, when the human race was in a more childish condition, he had legislated this strenuous way of life. Then we would never have accepted even the moderate one, and everything pertaining to our salvation would have been ruined by this excess. In the same way, if after that long time and the tutelage of the law, when the season was calling us to this heavenly philosophy, he had let us remain on the earth, we would have reaped no great benefit from that condescension, because the perfection for whose sake the condescension took place would never have come to us.

17. As it is, things have gone just as they do with nestlings. When the mother has reared them, she leads them out of the nest. But if she sees that they are weak and falling and still need to stay inside, she leaves them there for more days. She does this not so that they may stay inside forever, but so that, once their feathers are well set and they have gained their full strength, they may then take to flight safely. So too our Lord drew us toward heaven from the beginning and showed us the road that leads there. He was not unaware, but knew full well, that we would not be equal to that flight. He wished to show us that the fall happens not because of his will but because of our weakness. Once he had shown this, he let us be nourished for a long time in this world and in marriage, as in a nest. And when over that long time the wings of virtue had grown on us, he came gently, little by little, and led us out of our dwelling here, teaching us to fly higher. Those who are still sluggish and sleeping a deep sleep still linger fondly in the nest, nailed to the affairs of the world. But those who are truly noble and lovers of the light leave it with great ease and fly to the heights, and… [Note: Reg. reads “all the things of the earth… leaving [?]”.]

…the daughters of men, so great a destruction would not have overtaken them. And let no one think that I blame marriage for their destruction. That is not what I am saying now. I am saying that what destroys and corrupts our race is not virginity but sin.

19. Marriage, then, was given for the sake of having children too, but much more to quench the burning of nature. Paul is a witness to this when he says, “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife” — not because of having children. And again he commands them to come together, not so that they may become fathers of many children, but for what reason? “So that Satan may not tempt you,” he says. And going on, he did not say, “But if they desire children.” What did he say? “But if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry.” At the beginning, as I said, marriage had these two purposes. But later, when the earth and the sea and the whole inhabited world had been filled, only one reason for it remains: to do away with licentiousness and debauchery. Some even now wallow in these passions, wish to live the life of pigs and are ruined in brothels. For them marriage is of no small benefit, freeing them from that impurity and compulsion and keeping them in holiness and dignity. But how long shall I go on shadow-boxing? For you who say these things know as well as we do how far virginity excels, and everything you have said is a pretext, an excuse and a cloak for incontinence.

20. Even if it were possible to say these things without danger, you still ought to stop the slander. For anyone who sets his judgment against what is good does himself harm in other ways, and he also gives everyone no small proof of his own depravity in so perverse and unjust a verdict. So if for no other reason, you ought to restrain your tongue at least to avoid acquiring so wicked a reputation. Reflect that whoever admires those who shine in the greatest contests will be able to obtain pardon from everyone, even if he cannot attain the same himself. But someone who not only fails to pursue what deserves many crowns but also disparages it would justly be hated by all as an enemy and foe of virtue, and as worse off than the insane. For the insane do not know what they are doing, nor do they undergo what they suffer willingly. That is why, even when they insult people in power, they are not only not punished but are even pitied by the very people they insulted. But if someone dared to do these things willingly, when the insane do them unwillingly, he would justly be condemned by the votes of all as an enemy of our nature.

21. So, as I said, even if such an accusation carried no danger, you ought to abstain from it at least for the reasons I have given. But as it is, the matter also carries great danger. Not only will the one who sits and speaks against his brother and puts a stumbling block in the way of his mother's son be punished, but also the one who tries to slander things that God considers good. Listen to what another prophet says when he discusses this very thing: “Woe to the one who calls evil good and good evil, who makes light darkness and darkness light, who makes sweet bitter and bitter sweet.” For what is sweeter than virginity, what more beautiful, what more radiant? It sends forth rays brighter than those of the sun itself… [Note: Reg. and Savile read “will at least be able to obtain pardon.”]

…the praise that comes from God is all the consolation they need. But those who are weaker, and are only now being led by the hand into the undertaking, receive no small addition of strength even from the esteem of the many. This lasts until, trained little by little from every side, they bring themselves to the point of no longer needing this guidance. And this happens not only for their sake but also for the salvation of the very people who mock them, so that they do not advance further in wickedness through paying no penalty for what they did before. But while I am saying this, the memory of what happened in the time of Elijah has come to me. What the boys suffered from the bears because of Elisha, twice fifty men, together with their commanders, suffered because of his teacher, from fire kindled from above. For they too came with much mockery, called the righteous man and ordered him to come down to them. Instead of him, fire came down and devoured them all, no less than those beasts did. Consider this, then, all you enemies of virginity, and at last set a door and a bar on your mouths. Otherwise on the day of judgment, when you see those who shine there by virginity, you too may begin to say: “These were the ones we once held in derision and as a byword of reproach. We fools reckoned their life madness and their end without honor. How were they counted among the sons of God, and how is their lot among the saints? So we strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine on us.” But what will these words gain, when by then the time for repentance is past and it has lost all its strength?

22. But perhaps one of you will say, “So did no one after those times speak ill of holy men?” Many did, and in many places on earth. “Then how is it that they did not pay the same penalty?” he says. They did pay it, and we know of many of them. And if some escaped, they will not escape to the end. For as blessed Paul says, “The sins of some people are evident, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others follow after.” Lawgivers set down the punishments of wrongdoers in writing and leave it at that. In the same way our Lord Jesus Christ punished one or two of those who sinned and set out their punishments as though in letters on a bronze pillar. Through what happened to them he speaks to everyone, saying that those who dare the same things may not pay the same penalty in the present time as those who have paid it, but in the time to come they will undergo a harsher punishment.

23. So when we sin beyond measure and suffer no harm, let us not be confident. Let us rather be afraid for that very reason. For even if God does not judge us here, there we will be condemned with the world. And again, this verdict is not mine but that of Christ, who speaks in Paul. Addressing those who partake of the mysteries unworthily, he says: “For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and a number have fallen asleep. For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But now, when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned with the world.” For there are some who need only the rebuke given here, when their sins are moderate; once punished, they do not run back to their former ways, imitating the dog that returned to its vomit. There are others who, because of the excess of their wickedness, will pay the penalty both here and there. And others only… [Note: Reg., and the margin, read “So that when we sin much.”] [Note: Reg. reads “Sapphira, in the case of her husband, in the case of…”]

…lying upon the virgin. For these reasons, “it is good for a man not to touch a woman.” Then why do you permit touching? “Because of fornication,” he says. “I am afraid to lead you up to the height of virginity, in case you fall into the pit of fornication. Your wing has not yet become light enough for me to lift you to that summit.” And yet they themselves had chosen the contests and leapt into the contest of virginity. Why then do you fear and tremble, blessed Paul? Perhaps he would have said: “Because these people have this eagerness without knowing what the thing involves. But my own experience, and the fact that I have already engaged in this battle, make me more hesitant to advise others.

27. “I know the force of the thing. I know the strain of these contests. I know how heavy the war is.” What is needed is a soul that is combative and forceful, one that throws itself recklessly against the desires. For one must walk on coals and not be burned, and tread on a sword and not be wounded. The strength of desire is as great as that of fire and iron. If the soul is not prepared to pay no attention to the pains desire inflicts, it will quickly destroy itself. We need, then, a mind of adamant, an eye that never sleeps, much endurance, strong walls, battlements and bars on the outside, guards who are wakeful and brave, and, before all these, help from above. “For unless the Lord guards the city, the watchmen have kept watch in vain.” How then shall we draw this help to ourselves? By contributing everything we can on our own part: sound reasoning, fasting and vigils of great intensity, strict observance of the law, keeping of the commandments, and, chief of all, not trusting in ourselves. For even if we happen to have achieved great things, we must always say to ourselves, “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain.” “For our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” Our thoughts must stand armed night and day and be formidable to shameless desires. If they relax even a little, the devil stands ready with fire in his hands to throw it in and burn down the temple of God. We must therefore be fortified on every side. For our battle is against the necessity of nature; our zeal is for the life of the angels; we run our race alongside incorporeal powers. Earth and ashes strive to equal those who dwell in heaven, and corruption has entered into rivalry with incorruption. Tell me, will anyone still dare to compare marriage and pleasure with so great a thing? How could that not be utterly foolish? Paul knew all this when he said, “Let each have his own wife.” This is why he held back. This is why he did not venture to speak to them about virginity from the start but lingered over his words about marriage, wishing to draw them away from marriage little by little. He kept his words about continence brief and mixed them in among his many words about marriage, so that their ears would not be wounded by the [?]… [?] “…you permit, saying, ‘Because of fornication let each have his own wife.’” [?] “I wish to lead you to the height of [?], but I fear that you may fall.” [Note: Reg. and Savile read “I know the strain of these contests”; Morel, in the margin [?], reads “I know the strain of these virgins.”] [?] “to stand for our thoughts.” [Note: Reg. reads “if marriage.”]

29. So after saying, “The wife does not have authority over her own body,” he adds: “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer and fasting, and then come together again.” I think many of those who have embraced virginity blush here and are ashamed at how far Paul condescends. But do not be afraid, and do not react foolishly. These words do seem to come from someone indulging the married. But if you examine them carefully, you will find that they reflect the same mind as the earlier ones. If someone wished to read them simply, cut off from the reason behind them, they would seem to be the words of a matchmaker rather than of an apostle. But if he unfolds their whole purpose, he will find this exhortation too both timely and worthy of the apostle's dignity. Why does he dwell on this point at greater length? Had he not already indicated it more decorously in the earlier words? Would it not have been enough to stop his exhortation there? For what does “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time” contain beyond “Let the husband render to his wife the goodwill he owes her” and “The husband does not have authority over his own body”? Nothing more. But what was said there briefly and obscurely, he has worked out here at greater length and more clearly. In doing this he imitates Samuel, the holy man of God. Samuel expounded the laws of kingship to the common people with all precision, not so that they would accept a king but so that they would not. It seemed to be instruction, but in truth it was meant to turn them from their untimely desire. In the same way Paul keeps turning over the tyranny of marriage, more and more clearly, wishing by these very words to draw them away from it. For after saying, “The wife does not have authority over her own body,” he adds, “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement, so that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer.” Do you see how he has led those who remain in marriage into the practice of continence without arousing suspicion or giving offense? At the beginning he simply praised the thing, saying, “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” Here he has also added an exhortation, saying, “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement.” And why did he introduce what he wished to establish as an exhortation and not in the form of a command? He did not say, “Deprive one another, but by agreement.” What did he say? “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement.” He put it this way because it made his words gentler. It showed the mind of the teacher, which does not demand this vehemently, especially since the debt is paid most readily when it is paid with much good grace. And he does not console the hearer by this means alone. He also compresses the harsh part into a few words and, before the listener is pained, leaps over to the more pleasant things and lingers on them…

…It is also worth examining this question. If marriage is honorable and the marriage bed undefiled, why does he not allow it a place in the time of fasting and prayer? Because it would be quite absurd if the Jews took such care in this matter while we did not. Everything was laid down for them in bodily terms; they were permitted to have even two wives, and to put some away and take others in their place. Yet when they were about to hear divine words, they abstained even from lawful intercourse, and that not… [Note: Reg. reads “cutting off.”] [Note: Reg. reads “of instruction.”] [?] “…one another, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer, but not.”

So since we come to our prayers to quench so great a wrath, and to reconcile the one against whom we wage war every day, he rightly leads us away from that pleasure. He is all but saying: “Beloved, our concern is the soul; the danger concerns the ultimate things. We must tremble and fear and be humble. We are approaching a fearsome Master whom we have often insulted, who has great charges against us, and charges about great matters. This is no time for embraces or pleasures. It is a time for tears and bitter groans, for falling prostrate, for careful confession, for intense supplication, for much entreaty. For it is welcome enough if, falling down with such earnestness, we can approach that wrath and soften it. Our Master is not harsh or cruel; he is exceedingly gentle and loving toward humankind. But the excess of our sins does not allow even the kind, the gentle, the greatly merciful one to forgive us quickly.” That is why he says, “So that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer.” What, then, could be more bitter than this slavery? I want to advance in virtue, to fly up to heaven, to wash off the filth of my soul by persevering continually in fasts and prayers. But then, if she does not wish to consent to this purpose, I am forced to serve her lust. This is why he said at the start, “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” This is also why the disciples said to the Lord, “If this is how things stand between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.” They reckoned that one side or the other would necessarily be wronged, and, hard pressed by these thoughts, they uttered this cry.

33. That is also why Paul keeps returning to the point, so as to lead the Corinthians into this line of thought: “Let each have his own wife”; “Let the husband render to his wife the goodwill he owes her”; “The wife does not have authority over her own body”; “Do not deprive one another”; “Come together again.” For those blessed disciples did not react this way at the first word either. Only when they heard these things a second time did they perceive the constraint the commandment imposed. When Christ sat on the mountain he spoke about this, and after many other things he spoke of it again, and so led them into the love of continence. That is how the same things, said repeatedly, have greater effect. And here the disciple imitates the teacher and speaks again and again about the same things. Nowhere does he set down the concession simply; he always gives a reason, saying “because of fornication,” and speaking of the temptations of Satan and of incontinence. So, without arousing suspicion, he works the praise of virginity into his words about marriage.

34. If he is afraid to separate those living in marriage for long, in case the devil finds some way in, how many crowns must those women deserve who did not need this earthly consolation even at the beginning, and who remained unconquered to the end? And yet the devil does not even bring his devices to bear on both equally. I think he does not even trouble the married, because he knows that their refuge is near: if they feel a more violent assault, they can flee at once to the harbor. For blessed Paul does not let them sail very far out. He urges them to turn back whenever they grow weary, permitting them to come together again. But the virgin is forced to stay at sea the whole time and to sail an ocean without harbors. Even if the fiercest storm rises, not even then… [Note: [?] “soften.”] [Note: Reg. reads “‘Do you wish,’ he says, ‘to advance.’”] [Note: Reg. reads “forced to serve.”] [Note: Reg. reads “[?] will quench.”]

857 S. JOANNIS [?] hearing this, who would not be eager to escape the reproach of incontinence? For this exhortation is not addressed to everyone, but to those who are strongly inclined to sink low. "If you are such a slave of pleasures," he says, "if you are so slack that you are always poured out toward intercourse and gaping after it, then come together with your wife." So the concession is not that of one who approves or praises, but of one who mocks and condemns. For unless he had very much wished [?] to touch the souls of the pleasure-lovers, he would not have used the word "incontinence", which is the more forceful word and carries heavy reproach. Why did he not say, "Because of your weakness"? Because that would have been the word of one who pardons, while "incontinence" is the word of one who points out the extremity of slackness. So it is incontinence not to be able to keep from fornication unless one is always clinging to his wife and enjoying intercourse. What then would those who consider virginity superfluous say here? The more virginity is intensified, the greater the praise it earns; but marriage, when someone uses it to the point of satiety, is then most of all stripped of all praise. "For this I say," he says, "by way of concession, not of command"; and where there is concession, praise can have no place. "But when he speaks about virgins too, he says: I have no command of the Lord." Did he then perhaps put the two on an equal footing? Far from it! In the case of the virgin he gives an opinion; here he gives a concession. He commands neither, but not for the same reason. Here, it is so that someone who wishes to rise above incontinence is not held back as though bound by the necessity of a command; there, it is so that someone who cannot rise to virginity is not condemned as though disobeying an order. "I do not command you to remain virgins," he says, "for I fear how hard the thing is to achieve. I do not command you to come together with your wife continually, for I do not wish to be a legislator of incontinence. I said, 'Come together,' to keep you from going further down, not to hinder your eagerness to go further up." So it is not his primary wish that a man should always make use of his wife; rather, it is the incontinence of the more lax that laid down this law. For if you want to learn what Paul wishes, hear what it is: "I wish," he says, "that all men were as I myself am" — in continence. "So if you wish all to be in continence, you wish no one to be in marriage?" [?] "Yes; but I do not on that account hinder those who want it, nor do I accuse them. I pray and long for all to be as I myself am, but I also grant the other because of fornications. That is why at the outset I said, 'It is good for a man not to touch a woman': because this is what I long for more." 35. But why does he mention himself here, saying, "I wish that all men were as I myself am"? Surely if this had not been added, he would have escaped the charge of self-praise [?]. Why then did he add, "as I myself am"? Not to exalt himself. For he is the one who outdid the apostles in labors for the preaching, yet thought himself unworthy even of the title of apostle. Having said, "I am the least of the apostles," as if he had said something too great for his worth, he quickly checks himself, saying, "who am not fit to be called an apostle." Why then is this added to the exhortation here? Not idly or by chance; he knew that the disciples at that time most of all [?] … [Apparatus:] [?] to say "incontinence". he would not have contradicted both himself and Christ in this way: Christ, who says, "There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven," and adds, "Let anyone who can accept this accept it"; and himself, who condemns those women who chose widowhood but would not persevere in their resolve. For if it is a gift, why do you threaten them, saying, "They incur condemnation, because they have set aside their first faith"? Nowhere did Christ punish those who lack gifts, but everywhere those who do not show an upright life. And this is what he seeks most of all: excellent conduct and blameless works. The distribution of gifts, on the other hand, lies not in the choice of the one who receives but in the judgment of the one who gives. That is why Christ nowhere praises those who work miracles; rather, when the disciples were proud of this, he draws them away from such pleasure, saying, "Do not rejoice that the demons obey you." Those who are everywhere called blessed are the merciful, the humble, the meek, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, those who do all these things and things like them. And Paul himself, when he lists his own achievements, mentions continence among them. Having said, "In great endurance, in afflictions, in hardships, in distresses, in beatings, in imprisonments, in labors, in tumults, in sleepless nights, in fastings," he added, "in purity." He would not have done this if the thing were a gift. And why does he mock those who do not have it, calling them incontinent? Why does the man who does not give his virgin in marriage do better? Why is the widow more blessed if she remains as she is? As I said earlier, the beatitudes are for works, not miracles, and so are the punishments. And how could he keep on exhorting about these same things, if the matter were not in our power and did not require, after God's assistance, our own effort as well? Having said, "I wish that all men were as I myself am," in continence, he says again, "To the unmarried and to widows I say: it is good for them if they remain as I am." Again he puts himself forward, for the same reason: with an example close at hand and familiar to them, they would venture more boldly on the labors of virginity. And if both above, when he says, "I wish that all were as I myself am," and here, "It is good for them if they remain as I am," he nowhere adds a reason, do not be surprised. He does not do this out of arrogance, but because he thinks his own judgment, by which he himself accomplished the thing, is reason enough. 37. And if anyone also wishes to hear arguments, let him first examine the opinion of all people, and then what happens in such cases. Although lawgivers do not punish such marriages but allow and permit them, much is said against them by many [?], both in homes and in the marketplace, by people who mock, blame and turn away from them. Everyone shuns such people no less than oath-breakers, so to speak, not daring to make friends with them, nor to enter into agreements with them, nor to entrust them with anything else at all. For when they see them so easily casting out of their souls the memory of so much intimacy, friendship, companionship and partnership, a kind of numbness comes over them from these thoughts, and they will not receive them with full sincerity, regarding them as fickle and changeable. Nor is it only for these reasons that they shun them, but also for the sheer unpleasantness of what takes place. For what is more distasteful, tell me, than when, after so much wailing and lamenting and so many tears, and the squalid [?] … [Apparatus:] [?] "they shun". "having furnished, so that not even unwillingly" [?].

consolation; but after giving the others rest up to that point, he lets them go again, while her he leaves to stand continually without even a little breathing space, fighting throughout and pelted by desires, not allowing her to take even a short respite. For why did he not say to her too, "But if she does not exercise self-control, let her marry"? Because no one would say to an athlete, after he has thrown off his cloak, oiled himself, entered the stadium and sprinkled himself with dust, "Withdraw and flee your opponent." From then on he must do one of two things: leave crowned, or leave fallen and disgraced. In the training school and the wrestling ground, where the exercise is among one's own people and he grapples with friends as though with opponents, he is master of whether to toil or not. But once he has registered, the theater has filled, the president of the games is present, the spectators are seated, and his opponent has been brought in and drawn up against him, the law of the contests has taken that liberty away from him. So too with the virgin: as long as she is still deliberating whether she ought to marry or not, marriage carries no danger; but once she has chosen and registered, she has brought herself into the stadium. Who then will dare — when the theater is assembled, the angels watching from above, Christ presiding over the games, and the devil raging and gnashing his teeth, locked with her in the wrestling and gripped round the middle — to come forward and say: "Flee the enemy, give in to the labors, let go of your hold, do not throw or trip your opponent, but yield him the victory"? And why do I speak of virgins? No one would dare to utter this word even to widows, but instead that fearful one: "When they grow wanton against Christ and wish to marry, they will incur condemnation, because they have set aside their first faith." 39. Yet he himself says, "To the unmarried and to widows I say: it is good for them if they remain as I am; but if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry." And again: "If her husband falls asleep, she is free to be married to whomever she wishes, only in the Lord." How then does he punish the very woman he leaves free, and condemn as unlawful the marriage he says is in the Lord? Do not be alarmed: it is not the same woman, but another. Just as when he says, "If the virgin marries, she has not sinned," he is not speaking of the one who has renounced marriage — for it is plain to everyone that she has sinned, and sinned unbearably — but of the one who is still unmarried and has not yet decided for this or that, but remains between both lines of thought; so here too by "widow" he means the woman who simply has no husband and is not yet bound by the decision of her own choice, but is free to choose either this or that; while there he means the woman who is no longer at liberty to keep company with another bridegroom, but has entered the contests of continence. For it is possible to be a widow and yet not be enrolled in the order of widows, when one has not yet taken this on. That is why he himself says, "Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old, the wife of one husband." The widow in the simple sense he allows to marry if she wishes; but the one who has promised God to remain a widow forever, and then marries, he condemns severely, because she has trampled on her compact with God. she must endure; or, if she does not want this, she must flatter the man who abuses her and give herself over to him for whatever he wishes — whether to rain blows on her, or drench her with insults, or hand her over to the contempt of the servants, or anything else of the kind; for husbands have devised many ways of doing this when they wish to punish their wives. And if she will not bear these things, she must practice a fruitless continence. I call it fruitless because it does not carry the promise that belongs to it, since it arises not from a desire for holiness but from anger at her husband. "Let her remain unmarried," he says, "or be reconciled to her husband." "What then if he never wants to be reconciled?" she says. You have a second release and deliverance. What is it? Wait for his death. For just as it is never permitted for the virgin to marry, because her Bridegroom always lives and is immortal, so it is permitted for the married woman only when her husband dies. For if it were allowed, even while he lived, to leap from him to another, and from that one again to someone else, what need would there be of marriages at all, with men using one another's wives indiscriminately and everyone simply mingling with all? And how would affection toward those who share one's home not be destroyed, when today this man, tomorrow that one, and then another lives with the same wife? Rightly, then, did the Lord call this adultery. 41. How then did he permit it to the Jews? So that they would not make war on each other, so that they would not fill their houses with the blood of their own kin. For which was better, tell me: for the hated wife to be thrown out of the house, or to be slaughtered inside it? That is what they would have done if they had not been allowed to put her out. That is why he says, "If you hate her, send her away." But when he speaks to the gentle, whom he does not even allow to be angry, he says, "If she separates, let her remain unmarried." Do you see the necessity, the inescapable servitude, the bond that encloses both? Marriage truly is a bond, not only because of the throng of cares or the daily griefs, but because it forces the married to be subject to each other more harshly than any servant. "Let the husband rule over the wife," he says. And what is the gain of this mastery? For he in turn makes him the slave of the one he rules, devising a new and strange exchange of servitude. Just as the feet of runaway slaves, each bound on its own and then bound to one another by a short chain fastened at each end to the fetters, cannot walk freely, because one is forced to follow the other: so too the souls of married people have their own cares, but they also have another necessity arising from their bond to each other, which chokes them more harshly than any chain and takes away the freedom of both, since it does not hand authority once and for all to one, but divides power between the two. Where then are those who are ready to bear any condemnation for the comfort of pleasure? For no small part of the pleasure itself is cut off, since much time is often spent in quarrels and hatred toward each other. And this servitude — being forced to bear the other's wickedness, even against one's will — is enough to overshadow all delight. That is why that blessed man first checked the rush toward desire with shaming words, speaking of fornications and incontinence and burnings; but when he saw that the argument from condemnation counted for little with most people, he again [used] a stronger one than this toward [?] … [Apparatus:] Reg. ἐντείνοι, and just after, πλύνοι. and placing a blooming crown on their heads; but those who decline her and do not wish to join her, she neither punishes nor forces to do so against their will. Not only in this way did he make his words unburdensome and pleasant, but also by saying that the grace of the matter was not his own but Christ's. For he did not say, "Concerning virgins I do not command," but, "I have no command," as if to say: "If I were urging these things moved by human reasoning, you ought not to be confident; but since God decided this, the pledge of your security is sure. I have been deprived of the authority to command such things; but if you are willing to hear me as a fellow servant, 'I give my opinion,'" he says, "'as one who has received mercy from the Lord to be faithful.'" Here it is worth admiring the blessed man's great resourcefulness and good sense: caught between two things, both necessary and opposed to each other — to commend his own person, so that his counsel would be readily accepted, and yet to say nothing great about himself, since that would have been foreign to this virtue — he managed both in a few words. By saying, "as one who has received mercy," he commends himself in a way; by not doing so from the more splendid side, he humbles and restrains himself again. 42. For he did not say, "I give my opinion as one entrusted with the Gospel, as one deemed worthy to be herald of the Gentiles, as one entrusted with your oversight, as a teacher and guide." But how? "As one who has received mercy," he says, putting down the lesser thing; for to be merely a believer is less than to be a teacher of believers. And he devises yet another humility. What is it? He did not say, "as one who became faithful," but, "as one who has received mercy to be faithful." "Do not think that only my apostleship, my preaching and my teaching are God's gift; my very believing came to me from his mercy. It was not because I was worthy," he says, "that I was granted faith, but only because I received mercy"; and mercy belongs to grace, not to desert. "So if God were not exceedingly compassionate, I could never have become, not only an apostle, but even a believer." Do you see the servant's gratitude and contrite heart? He gives himself nothing more than the rest; even faith, which he had in common with the disciples, he says is not his own doing but the mercy and grace of God. By these words he shows the same thing, as if he were saying: "Do not disdain to receive counsel from me; for God did not disdain me as unworthy of his mercy. Besides, the matter is an opinion, not a command; I advise, I do not legislate. And no law would forbid anyone to bring forward and set out what seems beneficial to him, especially when this is done at the request of the hearers, as it is in your case." "I think, then," he says, "that this is good." Do you see again how subdued his words are, and how devoid of all authority? And yet he could have spoken like this: "Since the Lord did not command virginity, neither do I; but I advise and urge you to strive for it, for I am your apostle." Just as later, in speaking to them, he said, "If I am not an apostle to others, at least I am to you." But here he says nothing of the kind; he uses his words with great restraint, saying "I give my opinion" instead of "I advise," and "as one who has received mercy from the Lord to be faithful" instead of "as a teacher"; and as if not even these were enough to make his words modest [?] … [Apparatus:] Reg. and if one examines it in the household, he will find it full of the same difficulty and more, because of the wife. For a man must worry a great deal, and about many things he would not have needed to worry about if he were on his own — and that is when the wife is orderly and gentle. But if she is wicked, burdensome and unbearable, we will no longer call the thing merely a necessity, but a penalty and a punishment. How then will he be able to walk the road to heaven, which needs unencumbered, light feet and a soul well girded and nimble, when he has such a mass of affairs laid on him, is bound by so many fetters, and is continually dragged down by such a chain — I mean his wife's wickedness? 45. But what is the clever argument of the many, when we go through all these things with them? "Then the man who succeeds amid such necessity," he says, "will deserve greater honor." Why, my good man, and on what grounds? "Because he undergoes more toil on account of marriage," he says. And who forced him to take on such a burden? If he were fulfilling a commandment by marrying, and not marrying were a transgression of the law, this argument would be plausible. But if, being free not to come under the yoke of marriage, he chose of his own accord, with no one forcing him, to load himself with so many difficulties, so that the contest of virtue became more burdensome for him, that is nothing to the president of the games. For he commanded one thing only to be accomplished: the war against the devil, and the winning of victory over evil. Whether someone accomplishes this while married, living in luxury and full of cares, or while practicing asceticism and enduring hardship with nothing else to worry about, he is no longer concerned with that. As for the manner of victory and the road that leads to the trophy, he himself says it is the one freed from all the affairs of this life. But since you wish to serve as a soldier and fight with a wife and children and all the affairs they drag along with them, as though you would achieve the same as those entangled in none of these things, and would enjoy greater admiration for it — now, perhaps, you will charge us with great arrogance if we say that you cannot reach the same summit as they; but the end, and the time of the crowns, will then persuade you well that safety is far better than empty ambition, and that it is better to obey Christ than the vanity of one's own reasonings. For Christ says that even renouncing everything that belongs to us is not enough for virtue, unless we also hate ourselves; while you, mixed up in all these things, have claimed that you can prevail. But, as I said, then you will know well how great a hindrance to virtue a wife and a wife's cares are. 46. "How then," he says, "did he call her a helper, if she is a hindrance?" For he says, "Let us make for him a helper like himself." And I will ask you in turn: how is she a helper who robbed the man of such great security, cast him out of that wonderful life in paradise, and threw him into the turmoil of the present life? These are the acts not of a helper but of one who lays plots. For "from a woman," he says, "is the beginning of sin, and because of her we all die." …do I cut her off entirely from being an ally in spiritual things? God forbid! What I say is that she achieves these things when she does not busy herself with the affairs of marriage, but, while remaining a woman by nature, rises to the virtue of the blessed men. For it is not by adorning herself, or living in luxury, or demanding income from her husband, or being extravagant and costly, that she will be able to win him over. It is when she has risen above all present things and stamped the apostolic life upon herself, when she shows great gentleness, great modesty, great contempt for money, and patience under wrong, that she will be able to win him. It is when she says, "Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content"; when she practises this philosophy in her deeds, laughs at bodily death and declares the present life to be nothing; when she considers all the glory of this life to be, as the prophet says, the flower of grass. So it is not by living with him as a wife that she will be able to save her husband, but by displaying the life of the gospel. After all, many women have done this even without marriage. Priscilla, Scripture says, took Apollos aside and guided him into the whole way of truth. And if this is not permitted now, it is still possible among women to show the same zeal and reap the same gain. For, as I said before, even that wife does not draw her husband to herself because she is a woman. Otherwise nothing would have prevented anyone with a believing wife from remaining an unbeliever, if intercourse and living together were what accomplished the matter. But it is not so, it is not. What brings about the salvation of the spouse's soul is showing great philosophy and endurance, laughing at the troubles of marriage, and making this one's constant work. If she persists in pursuing what women usually pursue, not only does she do him no good at all, she actually harms him. And to see that even so the thing is among the very difficult ones, hear what he says: "For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?" We usually use this form of question about things that happen against expectation. And what does he say after this? "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be released. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife." Do you see how continually he makes his transitions, and how throughout he intermingles the two exhortations? Just as in his discussion of marriage he inserted words about continence, rousing the hearer along the way, so here too he again inserts words about marriage to give him a rest. He began from virginity, and before saying anything about it he immediately took refuge in the argument for marriage, for "I have no command" is the word of one who allows marriage and brings it in. "It is good for a person to remain as he is." And he does not even pursue the point, but cutting it off… [?] Reg.: "not by living with him as a wife to save." Reg.: "suddenly the [?] about."
