…and having learned the constraint that the yoke of marriage imposes, you may more readily accept the argument for remaining unmarried. "But if you marry," he says, "you have not sinned; and if the virgin marries, she has not sinned." See where the great achievement of marriage ends: in escaping blame, not in being admired. Admiration belongs to virginity; the married person must be content to hear that he has not sinned. "Why then," someone says, "do you advise people not to seek a wife?" Because once bound, one cannot be released; because the thing brings much tribulation. Tell me, is this all we shall gain from virginity, then, that we escape tribulation here? Who will endure virginity for such wages? Who would agree to enter so great a contest if, for all that sweat, he were to receive only this reward? What are you saying, Paul? You call me to fight demons (for our struggle is not against blood and flesh), you urge me to stand against the frenzy of nature, you exhort me, with flesh and blood, to achieve what the bodiless powers achieve, and you speak of earthly goods, and of our not having the tribulation that comes with marriage? Why did he not say, "If the virgin marries, she has not sinned, but she has deprived herself of the crowns of virginity, of its great and ineffable gifts"? Why did he not describe the good things stored up for virgins after the contest: how they go out to meet the Bridegroom, how they will have bright lamps, how with great glory and boldness they enter that bridal chamber together with the King, how, more than all others, they shine close to that throne and the royal chambers? Of these things he made not even a brief mention. Over and over he speaks instead of release from the hardships of life. "I think that this is good," he says, and instead of saying "because of the good things to come," he says "because of the present necessity." Then again, after saying, "If the virgin marries, she has not sinned," and keeping silent about the heavenly gifts she has deprived herself of, he says, "Such people will have tribulation in the flesh." And he does not do this only up to this point but right to the end. Neglecting to commend the thing by the good things to come, he again takes refuge in the same reason, saying, "The time is short." Instead of saying, "I want you to flash like lightning in the heavens and be shown far more brilliant than the married," here again he keeps to saying, "I want you to be free from care." Nor is it only here that he does this. When discussing patience under wrong, too, he took the same road of counsel. Having said, "If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink," having commanded so great a thing, ordering us to overcome the compulsion of nature and to stand against so great a fire [?], when he speaks of the reward he says nothing of heaven and the things in heaven but places the recompense in the harm done to the one who has wronged us: "For by doing this," he says, "you will heap coals of fire on his head." Why then did he use this way of exhorting? Not from ignorance, nor because he did not know how to attract and persuade the hearer, but because he, more than anyone, had mastered this virtue, I mean the art of persuasion. How is this clear? From what he said. How, and in what way? He was addressing Corinthians (we will speak later about what he said concerning virginity), Corinthians, among whom he had decided to know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified; to whom he did not [?]… [?] "to be admired" [?]. Shortly after, the same: "is content." [?] Ibid., the same: "full of sweat, if he receives this reward." Reg.: "after the [?]… to meet… the lamps… with great glory and boldness they enter into the." Reg.: "and he does not introduce the… but again." "But also" is missing in Reg.

…famines, diseases, wars, captivity, and all other such things. For the more carnal sort of people are gripped more by these and fear them more, and take less account of things unseen and not present. That is why Paul too dwells more on these things, which were best able to get through their dullness. Besides this, he also wanted to show that some of the other good things surround us with many labours here and store up all their fruit for the time to come, whereas virginity, in the very act of being achieved, gives us no small reward, freeing us from so many labours and cares. And along with these he established a third point. What was it? That the thing should not be thought impossible but entirely possible. He does this by showing, with great abundance of proof, that marriage has more difficulties. It is as if he were saying to someone: "You think this thing toilsome and laborious. But that is exactly why I say you should pursue it: it is so very easy that it gives us far fewer troubles than marriage. 'Since I am sparing you,' he says, 'and do not want you to have tribulation, for this reason I do not want you to marry.'" "And what tribulation?" someone may say. "On the contrary, we shall find that marriage holds much relaxation and luxury. First of all, satisfying desire with complete freedom and suffering no violence from nature is no small matter of ease. Then the rest of life is free of gloom and squalor and full of cheerfulness, laughter and joy. For people serve the flesh with a costly table, soft clothes, softer bedding, constant baths, perfumes, wine no worse than perfume, and much varied expense besides, and so provide it with great luxury."

50. Above all, not even these things are permitted. Marriage usually grants us freedom for intercourse alone, not for luxury as well. Blessed Paul is witness, saying: "She who lives in luxury is dead while she lives." If this was said about widows, hear what he says about married women too: "Women should adorn themselves in modest clothing, with all reverence and self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or costly garments, but, as befits women who profess godliness, with good works." And not only here but elsewhere too one can see him speaking at length so that none of these things should be eagerly pursued by us at all. But why do I speak of Paul? He said these things when it was the time of the highest philosophy and the grace of the Spirit was abundant. Amos was addressing the Jews, who were like children and were permitted luxury, extravagance and almost every superfluity. Hear how severely he attacks those devoted to luxury: "Woe to you who are coming to an evil day, who draw near and lay hold of false sabbaths, who sleep on beds of ivory and live wantonly on your couches; who eat kids from the flocks and suckling calves from the midst of the herds; who clap to the sound of the instruments; as though standing…" Reg.: "not even these things are permitted to marriage; for the [freedom] of intercourse…" and has: "[about] the married, what does he say? Women likewise in clothing…" "…eagerly pursued. 'For having food and clothing,' he says, 'with these we shall be content. Those who wish to be rich fall into foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction.' And why do I speak of Paul?" [?] "…how severely he mocked those devoted to luxury, saying."

…and her husband's male and female servants treat her with greater insolence. This class is suspicious and ungrateful anyway, and when it gains greater licence and sees its masters at odds with each other, it takes their war as no small occasion for its own villainy. For then they are free to invent and fabricate whatever they like with complete impunity, and to strengthen the suspicion with their slanders. A soul once seized by this wicked disease believes everything easily. Opening its ears equally to all, it cannot bring itself to tell slanderers from those who are not, and those who inflame the suspicion seem more trustworthy than those who try to tear it down. From then on she must fear and tremble before those runaway slaves and their wives no less than before her husband, giving up to them the rank that befits her and taking theirs instead. When, then, will she be able to live without tears? What night, what day, what festival will pass without groans, laments and wailing? Threats, insults and abuse never cease, some from the husband, who has been wounded for nothing, some from the vile servants. There are watches and guards, and everything is full of fear and trembling. Not only are her comings and goings pried into, but her words, her looks and her sighs are scrutinized with the utmost exactness. She must be more motionless than a stone, bear everything in silence, and be nailed to her chamber continually, worse off than a prisoner; or else, if she wants to speak, to sigh, or to go out, she must give account and explanation for everything to those corrupt judges, I mean the maids and the crowd of servants. Place among these terrors, if you like, untold wealth, a lavish table, herds of servants, a brilliant family, great power, much glory, illustrious ancestors. Leave out nothing of what seems to make the present life enviable, but gather it all carefully and set it against this grief, and the pleasure from those things does not even appear. It is obliterated, as a small spark that falls into a vast sea would surely be quenched. And this is when the husband is jealous. But if the passion should ever pass to the wife (and this happens not seldom), he will bear it more easily than the wife does, and the greater part of the pain again falls back on that wretched woman. She will not be able to use the same weapons against the one she suspects. Who will tolerate a wife ordering him to stay at home all the time? Which of the servants will dare to watch his master, and not be led off at once to the pit? She cannot console herself with these devices, nor by venting her anger in words. Once, perhaps, or twice, her husband will put up with her anger, but if she persists in constant accusations, he will quickly teach her that it is better to bear such things in silence and waste away. And this is when it is a matter of suspicion. But when the dreadful thing turns out to be true, no one will rescue the wife from the hands of the man she has wronged. With the laws on his side, he brings the one dearest to him of all into court and has her put to death. The husband, on the other hand, escapes the penalty of the laws, though he is reserved for the penalty from above, the verdict of God. But that is not enough to console that wretched woman; she must… Reg.: "abuse." Below, the same: "whatever they may wish, they are free." Reg.: "having given up the glory that befits them." Reg.: "and with [?] everything. For not."

…a servant instead of a wife; the free woman becomes a slave, and having lost the freedom of speech that belongs to her, she will be no better off than slaves bought with money. Whether he wants to live licentiously, to carouse in drunkenness, or even to bring a crowd of courtesans into her own bed, she must bear it all and even be glad of it, or else be thrown out of the house. And that is not the only dreadful thing. With her husband so disposed, she will not be able to give orders to the servants or the maids freely. As if she lived among other people's property and enjoyed what does not belong to her, living with a master rather than a husband, she is forced to act and to suffer in everything accordingly. But if a man wishes to marry a woman of equal standing, then equality of rank in turn spoils the law of subjection, since the measure of her wealth persuades her to put herself on a level with her husband. What then is one to do, when difficulty is everywhere? Do not, I beg you, bring forward the very few, easily counted marriages that have escaped these things. Things should be judged not by what is rare but by what always happens. In virginity it is hard for these things to happen, or rather impossible; in marriage it is hard for them not to happen.

56. If so many unpleasantnesses and misfortunes arise from what are thought to be blessings, what could one say about the things everyone agrees are painful? A wife does not fear only one death, although she herself will die only once, nor does she care for one soul, though she has only one. She trembles for her husband, she trembles for her children, she trembles for their wives and children in turn, and the more branches the root spreads into, the more her cares multiply. If any of them suffers loss of money, sickness of body, or any other unwelcome thing, she must beat her breast and lament no less than the sufferers themselves. If they all go before her, the grief is unbearable. If some remain and others are carried off by untimely deaths, not even then could one find unmixed consolation. For fear for the living, constantly shaking the soul, is no less than grief over the dead; indeed, if I may say something surprising, it is worse. Time softens despondency over those who have fallen asleep, but cares for the living must remain forever and cease only with death. And if our own sufferings are not enough for us, what kind of life shall we live, forced to mourn the misfortunes of others as well? Many women have been born of illustrious parents, raised in great luxury, and given in marriage to some very powerful man. Then suddenly, before they could be congratulated on these things, some danger fell upon them like a squall or a gale, and they too went down and shared the terrors of the shipwreck. Having enjoyed countless blessings before their marriage, they fell through marriage into the uttermost misfortune. "But these things," someone says, "do not usually befall everyone, nor always." Yet neither are they far from anyone (for I will say the same thing again). Some they reached through experience, and those who escaped the experience they distressed through anticipation. But every virgin is above both experience and anticipation.

57. However, if you agree, let us leave those things aside and now examine the things that nature has allotted to marriage, which no one can escape, whether willingly or unwillingly. What are they? Labour pains, childbirth and children. Or rather, let us take the argument further back, and the things before marriage… Not in Montfaucon's sense [?]: "although she will die alone." Edd. Reg.: "let us look into now."

[?] birth pangs [seize] a womb already worn out with toil, pangs which by themselves are enough to overshadow all the blessings of marriage. And along with these, other anxieties trouble her too. For the wretched, miserable young woman, though so violently racked by those pains, fears no less than them that the child may come out maimed and deformed instead of whole and healthy, or a girl instead of a boy. For at that moment this anxiety troubles women no less than the pangs themselves. Not only in matters for which they are answerable, but even in those for which they bear no blame, they fear their husbands no less than in the former; and, giving up all thought of their own safety in so great a storm, they worry that something unwelcome may befall the husband. And when the baby has dropped to the ground and uttered its first cry, other anxieties take over in their turn: anxieties about its survival, anxieties about its upbringing. If it happens to be gifted and well suited to virtue, the parents are again in fear that something terrible may happen to their child, that it may suffer an untimely death, that it may turn to some vice. For not only do good children come from wicked parents, but worthless and wicked ones come from virtuous parents too. And if any of these dreaded things happens, the grief is more unbearable than if it had happened at the start; and if all the good things remain secure, still the fear of change is always with them, shaking the parents' souls and cutting away a great part of their pleasure. "But not everyone who marries has children." Then you are giving me yet another reason for despondency. Since, then, whether they have children or not, and whether the children turn out good or wicked, they are gripped by griefs and anxieties of every kind, how can we go on calling married life the most pleasant? Again, if the couple go on living in harmony, there is the fear that death will strike and break up their pleasure; or rather, this is no longer merely a fear, nor does the calamity stop at expectation: it must absolutely come to pass in fact. For no one has ever been able to point to a couple who both died on the same day; and since this does not happen, the survivor must endure a life far harder than death, whether they lived together a long time or a short one. The one, the longer his experience of it, has the greater anguish, since long familiarity makes the separation unbearable; the other, deprived of that love before he could taste it and have his fill of it, while desire was still at its height, mourns for that very reason more than the first. So from opposite circumstances both are gripped by equal sorrows. And what need is there to speak of the separations that come in the meantime, the long journeys abroad, the anxieties that go with them, the illnesses? "And what has this to do with marriage?" someone says. A great deal: many women have often fallen ill precisely because of it. For when insulted and angered, sometimes from rage and sometimes from despondency, they have brought on many fevers. And even if they suffer nothing of the kind while the husband is at home, but enjoy his gentleness the whole time, his absence abroad brings them round again into these same ills. But let all this be set aside, and let us lay no charge against marriage; still, along with these we shall not be able to clear it of that other charge as well. Which one is that? That it leaves the healthy partner in no better state than the sick one, but brings him into the same despondency as the one lying ill. 58. Do you want us to throw all these things out too and suppose, for the sake of argument, [?] [Variant readings: Reg.: "for the safety and for the"; Reg.: "from circumstances"; Reg.: "sometimes by the husband, sometimes".]

[?] the pleasure that comes from being above those beneath her, the superiority of those above her [takes away]. "But the great luxury of gold, of clothes, of the table, and of freedom in everything else is enough to lure and draw the soul." And how many women enjoy these things? The greatest part of mankind lives with poverty, hardship and toil. And if there are some women who share in them, they are very few and easily counted, and even these do so against God's will; for no one is permitted to live in luxury in these things, as we showed in our earlier discourses. 61. But let us again suppose, for the sake of argument, that this luxury too is allowed, and that neither the prophet nor Paul is hostile to women who live in finery: what is the benefit of a great deal of gold? Nothing else but envy, anxiety, and no small fear. For it is not only when they put it away in the chest, nor only when night falls, that they are troubled with anxieties; when they wear it, too, and in broad daylight, they endure the same worry, or rather a worse one. For women who commit such crimes turn up at the baths and in the churches; and often, even apart from them, the women wearing gold are jostled and squeezed by the crowd and do not even notice when some of their gold falls off. In this way many have lost not only such things but necklaces far more precious still, made of precious stones, which were torn apart and fell off. 62. But let there be no such fear; let this anxiety too be removed: what is the benefit? "Someone else saw it," she says, "and admired it." But he admired not the woman wearing it but what she was wearing; and because of it he often even thought less of her, as adorned with it beyond her worth. If she is beautiful, it spoils her natural beauty: all that ornament does not let it appear unadorned, but takes away the greater part of it. If she is plain and ill-favoured, it makes her all the more unattractive. For plainness, when it is seen on its own, appears only as great as it is; but when the brilliance of stones and the beauty of some other material are set beside it, it is heightened into greater ugliness. Dark skin is shown up as much darker by the light of the pearl lying on it and gleaming as if in darkness; and ill-formed features are made to look much worse by the bright colours of the clothes, which do not let the shape of the face [?] compete on its own terms before the onlookers, but only against that handmade and extraordinary beauty, so that the defeat is all the greater. For the gold scattered over the garments, the great intricacy of the craftsmen who make such things, and all the rest of the finery are like a noble athlete in fine condition and full of vigour who has thrust aside some mangy, ugly, starving opponent: in this way the finery throws down the splendour of the wearer's face and draws the spectators to itself, making her the object of greater ridicule and itself the object of excessive admiration. 63. But the ornament of virginity is not like this. It does not spoil the one who wears it, since it is not bodily but belongs wholly to the soul. Therefore, if she is plain, it at once transforms her plainness by clothing her in extraordinary beauty; and if she is lovely and radiant, it makes her more brilliant [?] [Variant readings, partly illegible: Reg.: "superiority or glory" [?]; below, Reg.: "enjoying these" [?]; the same [?]: "lives with poverties, hardships and labours"; [?] "earlier discourses"; shortly after, Reg.: "Paul declared"; [?] "they will wear"; Reg.: "what is the benefit of wearing gold?" [?]; Reg.: "carried off" [?] [?].]

For what, tell me, does a virgin endure in her whole life that compares with what the married woman endures almost every year, broken by labour pains and wailing? So great is the tyranny of this pain that even divine Scripture, whenever it wants to allude to captivity, famine, plague and the most unbearable evils, calls all such things birth pangs. And God laid it on the woman as a punishment and a curse: not giving birth, I mean, but giving birth in this way, with pain and anguish. For "in sorrow," he says, "you shall bring forth children." But the virgin stands above this pain and this curse; for he who abolished the curse of the law abolished this one along with it. 65. "But being carried about the marketplace on mules is pleasant." This is merely superfluous, and devoid of all pleasure. Just as darkness is not better than light, nor being shut in better than being free, nor needing many things better than needing nothing, so neither will she be better off for not using her own feet. I pass over all the unpleasantness that must be endured as a result. For she cannot leave the house when she likes; often, even when some useful errand presses, she is forced to stay at home, like beggars whose feet have been cut off and who have nothing to carry them. And if her husband happens to have taken the mules out [?], there are petty resentments, quarrels and much sullen silence; and if she herself, foreseeing none of the consequences, does the same, she turns her anger away from her husband and against herself, continually gnawing at herself over the slight. How much better it would have been to use her feet (for that is why God made them for us) and endure none of these hardships, than to want to be pampered and be subject to so many causes of grief and pettiness! Nor are these the only reasons that keep such women at home: if the mules happen to go lame, whether both or one, the same thing happens; and when they have to be let out to pasture (which happens every year and for many days), she must again stay at home as if in chains, and not leave the house even when urgent business calls. And if anyone says that she is spared the crowd of people she would meet, since she is not forced to be seen by every acquaintance and to blush, he seems to me quite ignorant of what strips shame from a woman's nature and what clothes it with shame. For it is neither appearing in public nor keeping hidden that does this: the one is done by the forwardness that holds the soul within, the other by self-control and modesty. That is why many women free of that confinement, walking right through the crowd in the marketplace, have not only attracted no accusers but have won many admirers of their chastity, sending out the bright ray of their inner decorum through their bearing, their gait, and the simplicity of their clothing; while not a few of those who sit at home have wrapped themselves in an evil reputation. For it is possible, even while shut in, to display oneself to whoever wishes, with great forwardness and brazenness, more than the women who go out in public. 67. "But perhaps the crowd of maidservants is pleasant." Nothing is worse than this pleasure, so many anxieties does it bring; for one must be troubled and downcast over each one of them when she falls ill or dies. But perhaps these things are bearable, and even things harder than these, such as being strained every day [over their] laziness [?] [Variant readings, partly illegible: Reg.: "to her"; Reg.: "to be carried off"; [?] "shame" instead of "the shame"; [?] "the one holding within" [?]; after "pleasant" Reg. reads: "as many, then, as there are in the crowd; for it is necessary".]

[?] of the baths, and in the parks, and in houses, one can see that "mine" and "not mine" is nothing but a bare word. For the use of them is common to all, and those who are thought to own them have the advantage over those who do not only in the worry about them. The latter simply enjoy them, while the former, besides taking great pains over them, reap exactly the same benefit that the others reap without any care

69. And if anyone admires great luxury—the quantity of meat chopped up, the lavish spending on wine, the elaborate sauces, the skills of table-setters and bakers, the crowd of parasites and dinner guests—let him be well aware that in such matters the rich are no better off than their own cooks. For just as the cook fears his masters, so they fear their guests, lest they find fault with something prepared for them with much labour and expense. In this they are equal to the cooks, but in another respect they are worse off: they fear not only critics but also the envious. For envy has often been born in many people from such banquets, and has not stopped until it brought on the gravest dangers. "But eating a great deal is often pleasant." Away with that, when heaviness of the head, distension of the stomach, shortness of breath, dimness of sight, dizziness, fogginess and still stranger ills sprout from this luxury! And would that the disgrace and harm went no further than daily discomforts; but in fact the most incurable diseases have their origin in such tables. Gout, consumption, disease [?], paralysis, and many ills harder still take hold of the body and besiege it to its last breath. What pleasure, then, could anyone name that outweighs these evils? What austerity would anyone not choose to be rid of them? 70. But frugality is not like this; it stands far from these troubles and produces health and good condition. And if anyone is looking for pleasure, he will find this too in her, greater than in luxury: first, from being healthy and untroubled by those evils, each of which even by itself is enough to extinguish all pleasure and overturn it from its foundations; and second, from the food itself. How so? Because pleasure is produced by desire; and desire is produced not by satiety or surfeit but by want and scarcity. And this is always present, not at the banquets of the rich, but at those of the poor, dripping more honey on the dishes before them than any table-setter or cook. For the rich eat without being hungry, drink without being thirsty, and sleep before the need for sleep has come strongly upon them; whereas the poor first come into need of these things and only then partake of them, and this most of all is [the source] of pleasure. Why else, tell me, does Solomon say that the sleep of the servant is sweet, speaking thus: "Sweet is the sleep of the servant, whether he eats much or little"? Is it because of a soft bed? But most of them sleep on the floor or on a pallet of straw. Because of freedom? But they are not masters of even a brief moment of time. Because of ease? But they never stop being worn down by toil [?] [Variant readings, partly illegible: Reg.: "the skills of bakers and cooks"; Reg.: "to the servants" [?], others: "to the cooks"; Reg.: "the toils are pleasant"; "and first coming into need".]

[?] of the house, of tiles and of timber [?]. How then does he permit marriage, which nails us to other [?] [?] and by its anxieties draws us away from spiritual things? For this reason [?] let us not be anxious even now about the things of the earth; for the time calls us to [?], as the blessed Paul says, writing to the Romans: "For now our salvation is nearer than when we first believed [?]. The night is far gone, the day is at hand." And again: "The time is short; from now on let those who have wives be as though they had none." Why then [marriage] for those who will no more enjoy marriage than those who have none? Why money, why possessions, why the use of worldly things, when time is short and fleeting [?]? For if those who are about to stand before a court here among us and give an account of their offences, once the appointed day has come, withdraw from all care—not only for a wife, but even for food and drink—and think only of their defence, how much more must we, who are to stand not before an earthly court but before a heavenly tribunal, and to give an account of words and deeds and thoughts, withdraw from everything, from joy and from grief over present affairs, and be anxious only about that fearful day. "For if anyone," he says, "comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple; and whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple." Yet you sit idle, taken up with desire for a wife, with laughter and with luxury [?]? "The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything"; and you worry and fret about money? "The kingdom of heaven is at hand"; and you are concerned about a house and luxury and pleasure of every other kind? "The form of this world is passing away"; why then do you wear yourself out over the affairs of the world, which do not last but are being used up, while you neglect the things that last and are secure? No more marriage, no more birth pangs, no pleasure or intercourse, no wealth of money or care of possessions, no food or clothing, no farming or seafaring, no crafts or house-building, no cities or houses, but some other state and way of life. All these things will perish a little later. That is what "The form of this world is passing away" means. Why then, as though we were going to remain here for all ages, do we show such zeal, anxious about things we shall often part with before evening? Why do we choose the toilsome life when Christ calls us to the untroubled one? "For I want you," he says, "to be free from anxiety. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord." How then can you want us to be free from anxiety, when you cast us into other anxieties again? Because this is not anxiety, just as being afflicted for Christ's sake is not affliction—not because the nature of things is changed, but because the resolve of those who bear them is [full] of pleasure and masters the nature of things. For the man who is anxious about things he will not enjoy for long, and often not even for a short time, could rightly be said to be anxious; but the man who will receive fruits greater than his anxieties could with every justice be counted among those free from anxiety. And apart from this, so great is the difference between the two kinds of anxiety that this one is not even considered anxiety when compared with that one, so much lighter and so much easier is it. And all this we have shown in the preceding discourses. "The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, but the married man is anxious about the things of the world"; but the world passes away, while the Lord remains. Is this alone not enough to show the dignity of virginity? For as great as the difference between God and the world is, so much better is this care than that.

…she is in charge of cooks and weavers and the rest of the household staff. Far from it! The virgin gives no thought to any of these things. She cares for one thing [?] only: to build up her own soul, and to adorn that holy temple not with braids, gold or pearls, not with cosmetics or eye-paint, not with all the other tiresome and wretched contrivances, but with holiness of body and of spirit. "But the married woman," he says, "cares how she may please her husband." It was very wise of him not to go into the details. He did not list everything women suffer in body and soul to please their husbands: how they torment the body, plaster it with powder and stretch it on other tortures, and how they fill the soul with servility, flattery, hypocrisy, pettiness, and superfluous, useless cares. Instead he hinted at all this in a single phrase and left it to his hearers' consciences to reckon it up. Having thus shown how far virginity excels, and having raised it to heaven itself, he turns his discourse back to the concession of marriage, fearing at every point that someone might think the matter a command. That is why he was not content with his earlier exhortations. He had already said, "I have no command of the Lord," and, "If the virgin marries, she has not sinned," and here again he says, "Not that I may cast a noose upon you."

79. Here one might reasonably be puzzled. Earlier he called the matter a release from bonds. He said he gave this advice for our benefit, so that we might not have tribulation, so that we might be free from care, and because he spares us, and by all this he showed how light and bearable it is. How then can he say here, "Not that I may cast a noose upon you"? What does it mean? He did not call virginity a noose. Far from it! He meant choosing this good under force and compulsion. And so it is. Whatever a person accepts under compulsion and [?against] his will becomes more unbearable than anything, however light it may be, and chokes our soul worse than a halter. That is why he said, "Not that I may cast a noose upon you." In other words: "I have described and demonstrated all the goods of virginity, and yet after all this I leave the choice of the matter to you. I do not drag you to virtue against your will. I did not give this advice because I wished to afflict you, but so that seemly devotion might not be cut short by the affairs of life." Observe here too the wisdom of Paul: how he added exhortation to his disclaimers, and counsel through his concession. By saying, "I do not compel, but I exhort," and adding, "for what is seemly and for undistracted devotion," he showed how wonderful virginity is and how great a gain it brings us in the life that is according to God. A woman entangled in worldly cares and dragged about in every direction cannot be devoted without distraction, since all her zeal and leisure is divided among many things: I mean a husband, the care of a household, and everything else that marriage usually brings in its train.

80 [?]. What then, if [?] the virgin too is busy with many affairs and has worldly cares? Away with her! Drag her out of the choir of virgins! Not marrying is not enough [?] to make a virgin; there must also be purity of soul [?]. And by purity I mean not only being free of shameful desire and of adornment [?] … [?] (textual notes [?]: Reg.: "of her own to manage"; "having shown"; Reg.: "of a life dragged about everywhere because of undistracted devotion"; Reg.: "perished").

…of those who are ashamed of the matter. He does not attack him openly, but in praising the man who keeps his virgin he deals him a heavy blow. What does he say? "But he who stands firm in his heart." This is said in contrast to the man who is easily and readily swayed, who never knows how to walk steadily or stand with real courage. Then, since he saw that these words were enough to sting that man's soul, see how he shields him once more, by suggesting a cause that does not much deserve blame. Having said, "But he who stands firm in his heart," he added, "having no necessity, but having authority." Yet the natural thing would have been to say, "But he who stands firm and does not think the matter unseemly." That, however, would have stung more. So he put something else in its place to console him, and let him fall under this charge instead. For it is not as bad to hinder a virgin out of necessity as out of shame. The first belongs to an unmanly and wretched soul; the second to a perverted one as well, one that cannot even judge the nature of things rightly. But it was not yet the time for such words. Even when necessity presses, it is not right for a woman who has chosen virginity to be hindered; one must stand nobly against everything that cuts short this fine impulse. Hear what Christ says: "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." When we pursue anything pleasing to God, let whoever hinders us be counted an enemy and adversary, whether father or mother or anyone at all. But Paul, still bearing with the imperfection of his hearers, wrote, "But he who stands firm, having no necessity." And he did not stop the discourse there, even though "having no necessity" and "having authority" mean the same thing. By the length of his discourse and his string of concessions he consoles the poor, small mind, and to these he adds yet another reason: "who has decided in his heart." Being free is not enough, nor is a person accountable for this alone; but when he chooses and decides, then he does well. Then, so that you would not think the great condescension meant there was no difference, he sets out the difference again. He does it with reserve, but he does it nonetheless, saying, "So then he who gives in marriage does well, and he who does not give in marriage does better." Here, for the same reason as before, he did not show how much better. If you want to learn this, hear Christ saying: "They neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven." Do you see the difference, and to what height virginity lifts a mortal all at once, when it is truly virginity?

81 [?]. Tell me, in what did Elijah, Elisha and John, those true lovers of virginity, fall short of the angels? In nothing, except that they were bound to a mortal nature. In everything else, anyone who examines them closely will find them no worse disposed than the angels. And this very thing that seems a deficiency is a great reason for praise. They lived on earth and were subject to the constraints of mortal nature, yet they managed to reach that virtue. Consider how much courage, how much philosophy that required! That virginity made them what they were is clear from this: if they had had wives and children, they would not easily have lived in the desert, nor would they have despised home and all the other trappings of life. As it was, freed from all these bonds, they lived as though they were in heaven, upon [?] … (textual notes [?]: "nor wine-presses"; Montf.: "nor meadows"; Reg.: "only free").

…to speak of the things of this life [?]. That is why Paul called it the root of all evils. But virginity can dry up this root and plant another in us, the best one, which puts forth every good thing: freedom, boldness, courage, fiery zeal, a warm love of heavenly things, and contempt for everything on earth. This is how "what is seemly and undistracted devotion" comes about.

82. But what is the clever argument of the many? "The patriarch Abraham," someone says, "had a wife and children, money, flocks and herds. And after all that, John the Baptist and John the Evangelist, both of them virgins, and Paul and Peter, who shone in continence, pray to come into his bosom." Who told you this, my good man? What prophet, what evangelist? "Christ himself," he says. "When he saw the centurion with his great faith, he said, 'Many will come from east and west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.' And Lazarus too is seen by the rich man enjoying delight with him." And what has this to do with Paul, or Peter, or John? Lazarus was not Paul or John, and the many from east and west were not the choir of the apostles. So this argument of yours is superfluous and empty. If you really want to hear the prizes of the apostles, hear the one who is to give them, as he says: "You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." Here there is no mention of Abraham, or his son, or his son's son, or the bosom that received them, but of a dignity far greater than that, for these will sit in judgment on their descendants. Nor is the difference clear only from this, but also from the fact that what Abraham obtained, many will obtain: "Many will come," he says, "from east and west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob." But no one else will lay hold of those thrones; only [?] this choir of saints. Tell me, do you still talk of flocks and herds, marriages and children? "What then," he says, "when many of those who have lived as virgins pray, after all their toil, to go there?" I will say something stronger: many who have lived as virgins will not even obtain that bosom, nor anything lesser, but will go off into Gehenna itself. The virgins shut out of the bridal chamber show this. Is marriage then equal to virginity on this account, or is virginity even worse? Your example does make it even worse. For if Abraham, who married, is at ease and in delight, while those who lived as virgins are in Gehenna, then by your argument that is all one can suspect. But it is not so, it is not! Virginity is not only not inferior to marriage; it is far better. How so? Marriage did not make Abraham what he was, and virginity did not destroy those wretched women. It was the rest of his soul's virtue that made the patriarch illustrious, and the rest of their life's wickedness that handed those women over to the fire. Even while living in marriage, he strove to achieve the goods of virginity: I mean what is seemly and … [?] (textual notes [?]: "You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory, you also will sit on [?]…"; Reg.: "but only"; Ald.: "we fall short").

…age, once they have become men and do these things, we no longer admire them in the same way; we bid them show other things far greater. In the same way God did not demand great achievements of human nature in the early times, since it was still in a rather childish state. But once it had heard prophets and apostles and received the grace of the Spirit, he raised the scale of its achievements, and rightly so. For he has set greater rewards, and the prizes are now far more splendid. No longer is it the earth and what is on the earth, but heaven and goods beyond understanding that are laid up for those who succeed. How then is it not absurd to stay in the same smallness now that we have grown to manhood? In those days human nature was divided against itself, and there was a war without truce. Paul describes it somewhat like this: "I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind, and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members." But now it is not so: "For what the law could not do, weak as it was through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh." And giving thanks for this, Paul said: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ." So we are rightly punished, because we who have been set free are not willing to run as fast as those who were in shackles. Or rather, even if we managed to run as fast, not even then would we escape punishment. For those who enjoy deep peace, compared with those heavily weighed down by war [?] … much greater [?] … a person must, along with virginity, practise all the rest of virtue as well and set up more splendid trophies. But if we are going to [?] about virtue, so that after our departure from here [?] useless money and luxury and women and [?] … (textual notes [?]: another reading: "So also human nature"; Reg. ends at these words; another reading in the margin: "than those heavily weighed down by severe wars"; [?]).
